Short answer: the bulge domain is placed in fold b.84 (Barrel-sandwich hybrid) because it shares that fold's architecture, two half-barrel-shaped beta-sheets packed into a sandwich, but it is given its own superfamily rather than being folded into b.84.1, b.84.2 or b.84.3 because there is no evidence that it shares a common ancestor with any of them. The placement therefore asserts structural similarity only, and explicitly denies homology.

What the domain is. The A (catalytic) subunit of V1/A1-type ATP synthases (SCOP representative: Pyrococcus horikoshii A subunit, PDB 1vdz; later A-subunit structures, e.g. from Methanosarcina mazei and Enterococcus hirae, carry the same element) is a paralog of the F1 alpha/beta subunits and is cut into the same three homologous domains: an N-terminal six-stranded beta-barrel (b.49.1, 'N-terminal domain of alpha and beta subunits of F1 ATP synthase'), a P-loop/RecA-like nucleotide-binding domain (c.37.1), and an all-alpha C-terminal domain (a.69.1). In addition, the A subunit has a roughly 90-residue insertion within the N-terminal barrel region, the 'non-homologous region' (NHR) or bulge, that has no counterpart in F1 alpha/beta or in the V1 B subunit. SCOP excises this insertion as a fourth domain and classifies it in fold b.84 as a separate superfamily (named for the bulge domain of the V1/V-type ATP synthase A subunit) with a single family and, in SCOP 1.75/SCOPe, essentially a single protein entry.

Why a separate superfamily and not a family inside an existing one. In SCOP/SCOPe the fold level means only that domains have the same major secondary-structure elements in the same arrangement and topology; the superfamily level is the lowest level at which common ancestry is asserted (low sequence identity but structural and functional features suggest a common evolutionary origin), and the family level requires clear evidence such as >30% identity or very similar structure plus function. The established b.84 superfamilies are (i) b.84.1 Single hybrid motif, the biotinyl/lipoyl carrier domains of acyl-carrier proteins and biotin/lipoate-dependent enzymes (e.g. BCCP, E2 lipoyl domains, H-protein), (ii) b.84.2 Rudiment single hybrid motif, the BC C-terminal-domain-like domains of biotin carboxylase, carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase and pyruvate carboxylase, which are a degenerate half of the biotinyl motif, and (iii) b.84.3 Duplicated hybrid motif, e.g. the urease beta subunit, where the motif is tandemly duplicated. These groups are related to one another by sequence motifs (the conserved Lys-carrying hairpin, the 'hammerhead' extensions) and by a shared functional context in carboxylation/acyl-transfer chemistry. The ATP synthase bulge has none of this: its sequence shows no detectable similarity to the hybrid-motif proteins, it has no biotin/lipoyl attachment lysine or swinging-arm function, it occurs in a completely different protein context (a rotary ATPase catalytic subunit, where it probably contributes to stator/subunit contacts or to the A/B interface), and it is phylogenetically restricted to V/A-type A subunits. With only a shared sandwich-of-half-barrels topology and no sequence, motif, or functional support, the SCOP curators had no basis to assert descent from the hybrid-motif lineage, so the domain was left at fold-level membership only, as its own superfamily.

The evolutionary claim. Putting the bulge in b.84 but in a distinct superfamily makes two claims at once. First, the barrel-sandwich hybrid architecture is a recurrent fold that has arisen (or been retained) in at least two unrelated lineages; the bulge is treated as an independent, probably convergent, instance of the fold rather than a diverged descendant of the biotinyl/lipoyl carrier module. Second, because homology is asserted only at the superfamily level and below, nothing known about b.84.1/b.84.2/b.84.3 may be transferred to the bulge: no inference of a biotin/lipoyl-binding ancestor, no functional annotation (carboxyl/acyl transfer, cofactor attachment), and no justification for using hybrid-motif structures as homology-modelling templates or for building a shared sequence profile across the superfamilies. Conversely, the bulge is also not treated as homologous to the rest of the A subunit; it is an insertion into, not a derivative of, the b.49.1 barrel, so it tells us nothing about the ancestry of the F1/V1 catalytic subunits beyond the fact that the V/A lineage acquired an extra domain after the alpha/beta/A/B paralogs diverged.

Limits. (1) The exact superfamily number within b.84 for the bulge should be checked against the current SCOPe release; what is secure is that it is a separate superfamily under fold b.84, not a family under b.84.1-b.84.3. (2) The separate superfamily is a conservative, evidence-based decision from SCOP 1.73/1.75; it is a statement of no detected homology, not proof of independent origin. If sensitive profile-profile or structure-based methods in the future revealed a shared ancestry, SCOPe's manual curation could merge superfamilies, but SCOPe 2.x releases have kept the SCOP 1.75 hierarchy and add new entries only into existing families by automated methods, so the bulge superfamily remains as curated. (3) Representative-selection caveat: this superfamily is populated by essentially one protein (the archaeal A subunit, with additional A-subunit structures assigned to the same node), so any 'superfamily-level' statistics or benchmark sampling drawn from it reflect a single lineage, and the domain boundary (an excised insertion) means the SCOPe domain is discontinuous from the parent chain's other domains.
